newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Jobless claims, Philly Fed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Jobless claims, Philly Fed.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market could advance farther on Thursday if weekly jobless claims figures and the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's report on area business conditions fit the soft economic data pattern, analysts said.
After a well-bid five-year Treasury note auction helped to extend a rally on Wednesday, the 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond rose 11/32 to end at 101-6/32, its yield down to 6.41 percent.
Analysts said the market's advance could abate next week before the Thanksgiving Day holiday weekend.
"This has all the hallmarks of being a major bond market rally and the gains could continue on Thursday," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

"It appears as though there will be some pretty good demand from a broad base of customers," agreed Chris Iggo, chief financial economist at BZW Securities Inc. "The fundamentals are supportive. The economic data are soft."
Rupkey said the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's November survey of area business conditions, due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, could be key to the market's performance.

Economists Reuters polled estimated, on average, a 5.0 reading for the survey, little changed from October's reading of 5.3 and a reading consistent with the notion of a sluggish manufacturing sector.
Rupkey said the Philadelphia Fed survey as a tool to try to tell where the economy is had slipped in market importance.
In 1994, the price component of the Philadelphia Fed survey was a key piece of data for the market, Rupkey said.
"But the relationship between NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management index) and the Philadelphia Fed has gotten a little loose," said Rupkey.
"The claims data and the Philly Fed survey will be watched, of course, but it seems that most people expect the Philly Fed to be soft," said Iggo.
A negative reading on the Philly Fed would emphasize slowing manufacturing activity and would spur more buying in the credit markets, said Rupkey.
"Certainly, if it goes into negative territory, it will just add fuel to the fire," said Rupkey.
"People will watch the Philly Fed," agreed Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust, and the weekly jobless claims will also be interesting.

"Jobless claims have been the one piece of data that really haven't confirmed any kind of significant slowdown in the labor market so it will be interesting to see if they fall in line (with other economic figures)," said Feinman.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that jobless claims in the week ended November 16 totaled 332,000, up from 328,000 a week earlier.

From a technical point of view, the question is whether the market has the will to close below 6.38 percent on the long bond yield, a level the market hasn't seen since the close earlier this year on March 5.
The high for the bond on Wednesday was 101-11/32. A 30-year bond yield of 6.375 percent would correspond to a price of 101-21/32, an important psychological resistance area, said Rupkey.
If the market reaches that level, it will likely stop there before the Thanksgiving Day holiday, said Rupkey.
"Already people are talking about not being in for part of next week," he said.
Dealers indicated that Fed funds would open between 5-1/4 percent and 5-5/16 percent on Thursday.
